guideline_source: ADA Standards of Care 2024 + Joint British Diabetes Societies
description: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a life-threatening complication of diabetes characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and acidosis. Requires aggressive IV fluids, insulin, and electrolyte management.

decision_rules.description: DKA with severe acidosis, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability

action.procedure: ICU admission, aggressive fluid resuscitation, IV insulin
action.rationale: Severe DKA mortality 5-10%, requires ICU-level care

decision_rules.evidence_text: Severe DKA (pH < 7.0, HCO3 < 10, altered mental status) requires ICU admission. Mortality increases with severity of acidosis and presence of precipitating illness.

action.procedure: Hospital admission, IV fluids, insulin drip
action.rationale: Moderate DKA can progress to severe if not treated promptly

decision_rules.evidence_text: Moderate DKA (pH 7.0-7.24, HCO3 10-14) typically managed in step-down or floor with close monitoring. Requires IV insulin and aggressive hydration.

action.procedure: Hospital admission, IV fluids, subcutaneous insulin possible
action.rationale: Even mild DKA requires hospital management

decision_rules.evidence_text: Mild DKA (pH 7.25-7.30, HCO3 15-18) may be treated with subcutaneous insulin analogs in select patients, but most require IV insulin.

decision_rules.description: Classic triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and acidosis

criteria.name: Ketosis
criteria.definition: Positive serum or urine ketones, beta-hydroxybutyrate > 3 mmol/L

decision_rules.evidence_text: DKA diagnostic criteria: Blood glucose > 250 mg/dL (though euglycemic DKA can occur), serum ketones positive, arterial pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, anion gap > 12.

action.rationale: Clinical picture consistent with DKA - confirm with labs

decision_rules.evidence_text: Classic DKA symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid), fruity breath odor (acetone).

decision_rules.description: Risk of cerebral edema during DKA treatment

action.procedure: Mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV, reduce fluids, elevate head, neurosurgery consult

decision_rules.evidence_text: Cerebral edema occurs in 0.5-1% of pediatric DKA, mortality 21-24%. Risk factors: young age, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, high BUN, rapid fluid administration. Signs: headache, altered mental status, bradycardia, hypertension, pupil changes.

text_chunks.title: DKA Diagnosis Criteria
text_chunks.content: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) Diagnostic Criteria: (1) Blood glucose > 250 mg/dL (though euglycemic DKA can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors or pregnancy), (2) Arterial pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, (3) Positive serum ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate > 3 mmol/L preferred) or positive urine ketones, (4) Anion gap > 12. Severity classification: Mild (pH 7.25-7.30, HCO3 15-18), Moderate (pH 7.0-7.24, HCO3 10-14), Severe (pH < 7.0, HCO3 < 10).

text_chunks.title: DKA Treatment Protocol
text_chunks.content: DKA Treatment Protocol: (1) IV Fluids: NS 1-1.5L in first hour, then 250-500 mL/hr based on hydration status. Switch to D5 1/2NS when glucose < 200. (2) Insulin: Regular insulin 0.1 U/kg bolus, then 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion. Goal glucose drop 50-70 mg/dL/hr. (3) Potassium: If K < 3.3, hold insulin, replace K first. If K 3.3-5.3, add 20-30 mEq K to each liter. If K > 5.3, check q2h. (4) Bicarbonate: Only if pH < 6.9. (5) Monitor BMP, glucose q1-2h until stable.

text_chunks.title: DKA Red Flags
text_chunks.content: Red flags in DKA requiring ICU admission: (1) pH < 7.0, (2) HCO3 < 10, (3) Altered mental status (stupor, coma), (4) Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors, (5) Anion gap > 25, (6) Serum osmolality > 320, (7) Precipitating illness requiring ICU (MI, sepsis, stroke), (8) Failure to improve after 4-6 hours of standard treatment. Cerebral edema signs: headache, altered mental status, bradycardia, hypertension, pupil changes.

text_chunks.title: DKA Precipitants and Prevention
text_chunks.content: Common DKA precipitants: (1) Infection (30-50%) - UTI, pneumonia, skin infections, (2) Non-compliance with insulin (20-40%), (3) New-onset Type 1 diabetes (20-25%), (4) Medications - steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors, antipsychotics, (5) Acute illness - MI, stroke, pancreatitis, (6) Substance abuse - alcohol, cocaine. Prevention: Sick day rules education, ketone monitoring, never stop long-acting insulin completely, seek care early.

text_chunks.title: DKA vs HHS vs Other
text_chunks.content: Differentiating DKA from HHS and other conditions: DKA: BG > 250, pH < 7.3, ketones positive, anion gap elevated, younger patients, Type 1 or insulin-deficient Type 2. HHS: BG > 600, pH > 7.3, minimal ketones, osmolality > 320, older patients, Type 2, more profound dehydration, higher mortality. Euglycemic DKA: glucose < 250 but ketoacidosis present, seen with SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, starvation. Alcoholic ketoacidosis: history of alcohol binge, low/normal glucose.
